title: Swapback + Prefetch Throttle — Lab Notes
content:
Summary:

This is a lab notebook summarizing a focused investigation into an observed class of p95+/tail latency spikes tied to background page reclamation (swapback) when multi-tenant KV cache residency crosses certain thresholds. The investigation explores: (1) how aggressive prefetch increases reuse but can trigger swapback under high aggregate resident set growth, (2) the interaction with memory bandwidth saturation, and (3) whether a rate-limited prefetch throttle can reduce tail without sacrificing overall reuse-derived cost savings.

Why this matters (observed symptom):
- Intermittent 99p token latency regressions during mixed short and long-chat workloads.
- Correlated host-level metrics: non-trivial increases in stall cycles, spikes in page-faults/sec, and short (~100-300ms) throughput dips at the same times.
- Reproducible in staging with synthetic mixed workload at ~1.6x baseline concurrency.

Hypothesis statements:
1) Heavy prefetch aggressiveness increases KV resident set quickly; when the resident set growth contends with other processes or NUMA frictions it causes kernel swapback/paging pressure, leading to transient stalls.
2) Memory bandwidth (GB/s) saturation amplifies the latency impact because prefetch reads + eviction writebacks compete for DRAM channels.
3) Introducing a rate limiter on prefetch issuance (tokens/sec with burst window tied to observed bandwidth headroom) will smooth resident growth and reduce tail latency while retaining most reuse benefits.

Bench setup and reproducible steps:
- Cluster: 4x p4d-like nodes (8 GPUs total), OS: Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15, numa-aware allocator enabled in runtime.
- Model: Llama-like 13B variant with kv cache per request, typical sequence length mix: 64 (60%), 512 (30%), 1024 (10%).
- Workload generator: replay-preserving session mix via local harness (scripts/repro/swapback-mix-run.sh).
- Baseline config: prefetch on, predictor threshold T=0.7 (aggressive), prefetch window=8 pages, kv-reservation disabled.
- Measurement: per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), host pmu counters (LLC misses, mem BW via perf stat), kernel page-faults, free memory over time, and resident set tracked by runtime telemetry.

Key experiments and results (short-form):
1) Baseline aggressive prefetch (T=0.7):
   - Reuse rate: +31% (tokens avoided from model recompute)
   - p99 latency: +220ms median increase vs conservative baseline
   - Page-fault spikes: up to 400/s during bursts
   - Observed memory bandwidth: sustained ~85% of device channel capacity on hotspot NUMA node
   - Notes: Large reuse wins but large tail regressions; eviction write-back rate high.

2) Conservative prefetch (T=0.3, window=2):
   - Reuse rate: +8%
   - p99 latency: improved (40–60ms lower than baseline) but steady p50 similar
   - Bandwidth: ~45% utilization
   - Notes: Lower tail but lose most reuse benefit.

3) Rate-limited prefetch (token bucket limiter in runtime):
   - Config: 400 prefetch-ops/sec token rate, burst capacity 1200 ops, dynamic token refill adjusted by observed mem BW headroom sampled every 250ms.
   - Reuse rate: +24% (close to aggressive)
   - p99 latency: +30–55ms vs conservative baseline (far better than aggressive)
   - Page-faults: reduced peak to <120/s
   - Bandwidth: averages ~62% with short spikes well-contained
   - Notes: Sweet spot — preserves most reuse while containing resident set ramp-up and writeback pressure.

4) Bandwidth-throttled prefetch (heuristic tied to perf counters):
   - When mem BW > 75%, prefetch paused; resumed when <60%.
   - Reuse rate: +21%
   - p99 latency: similar to rate-limited approach, slightly noisier due to abrupt on/off behavior.

Profiling artifacts and specific signals we used:
- perf stat counters: LLC-load-misses, LLC-store-misses, cycles-stalled-frontend/backend, and mem-loads to estimate read amplification.
- runtime telemetry: eviction-rate/sec, prefetch-requests/sec, resident-bytes-per-tenancy, per-request kv-hit-ratio.
- kernel: /proc/vmstat (pgfault, pgmajfault), slab stats for page cache growth.
- NUMA traces: numastat and node-local memory allocation hotspots.

Small trace excerpt (runtime telemetry timeline snippet):
- t=00:01:22 prefetch-ops/sec=1370 resident-gb=72 eviction-ops/sec=540 mem-bw=312GB/s pgfault/sec=368 --> transient p99 spike
- t=00:01:24 prefetch-ops/sec=420 resident-gb=69 eviction-ops/sec=210 mem-bw=240GB/s pgfault/sec=90 --> tail cleared

Root cause analysis summary:
- Aggressive prefetch accelerates resident set expansion; when combined with bursty long sequences it increases asynchronous eviction writebacks and competes for memory bandwidth.
- The kernel's reclaim path (swapback-like behavior) is invoked when available pagecache/RSS headroom drops, producing short stalls as pages are pinned/cleaned.
- NUMA cross-node allocation (observed on some hosts) significantly increases writeback latency and exacerbates tail.

Mitigations & proposals (practical ideas tested):
1) Add a rate-limiter at prefetch issue point (token bucket) — proved effective in lab.
2) Implement bandwidth-aware adaptive throttle: sample DRAM channel utilization and reduce prefetch if above threshold.
3) Soft-reservation: allow lightweight reservation for hot sessions so their prefetches are prioritized under contention (helps PLG tail-sensitive customers).
4) Tune eviction writeback batching to avoid creating synchronized write spikes (stagger commit times across GPU processes).
5) NUMA-aware allocation heuristics: prefer local node allocations for prefetch pages; trigger cross-node prefetch only when local headroom < X.

Open questions and next steps:
- Long-term: can we bake a predictor that projects resident growth per-window to proactively throttle prefetch before kernel reclaim? Need a small forecasting model (exponential smoothing) instrumented in the runtime.
- Need more production-like runs across 8–12 node clusters and with Dedicated reserved workloads to ensure behavior under different tenant mixes.
- Explore hybrid approach: aggressive prefetch for low-cost tiers, conservative for high tail-SLO tenants via routing policy.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: land token-bucket prototype in prefetch path and add telemetry (PR drafted, see linked PR). (ETA: 2 weeks for initial canary)
- Daniel: run expanded scale experiments across staging cluster with dedicated NUMA forcing and capture perf counters. (ETA: 1 week)
- Lina: draft runtime knob docs and recommended defaults for Hosted vs Dedicated. (ETA: 1 week)
- Ethan: investigate writeback batching changes and coordinate with infra for kernel reclaim flags to test. (ETA: 3 weeks)

Notes-to-self / loose thoughts:
- Watch for interactions with KV spillback — if we start throttling prefetch heavily, we may increase compute cost; ensure downstream cost alerts are tuned.
- Consider a simple chaos test that injects delayed writeback to simulate noisy neighbors and validate throttle resilience.
- Keep the early canary on low-traffic pool until we have better confidence; capture end-to-end token cost delta as part of canary metrics.

- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/378 (prefetch rate limiter prototype)
- Slack: #eng-runtime thread (for traces)
